paras: The Polk City train mob was an attempt by vigilantes at Polk City, Iowa, on the evening of April 17, 1882, to seize men arrested for the murder of the town's mayor, R. W. Stubbs, from a train taking them to the Des Moines jail. The vigilantes took one prisoner off the cars before citizens persuaded them to let the train leave, and no one was killed. Wire reports of a lynching went out and were denied the next day, and the story ran under headlines such as "Murderers Saved from Lynching."

Stubbs, the mayor of Polk City, was shot in his house early on Saturday, April 15, 1882, by a burglar or burglars, according to the dispatches. Wires named Job Weise, John Swin and Charles D. Errikson as "the parties arrested as burglars and the murderers" of Stubbs, while a Des Moines dispatch carried in Portland counted five arrests with one suspect still at large. None of the accounts gives the race of the prisoners.

Stubbs's funeral was held on April 17 with the Odd Fellows and the United Workmen in charge and a procession said to be more than a mile long. Vigilantes guarded the prisoners until train time that evening, when they "reluctantly surrendered" them to officers, according to the National Associated Press. Once the prisoners were aboard, the vigilantes rallied, boarded the train, opened the switch and put a man with a revolver at each brake, declaring that the prisoners should not be taken away.

One prisoner was taken from the cars and efforts were made to get the others. The National Associated Press credited a traveling salesman named Read, of the Des Moines firm Oberne, Hosick & Co., who mounted a barrel and made "an eloquent plea for law and justice", while the Portland version said prominent citizens appealed to the leaders. The train was allowed to leave, and the prisoners were lodged in the county jail at Des Moines for safe keeping.

No report of arrests or charges against the vigilantes appears in the coverage. By early May an Iowa paper wrote that the burglar might never be found and that "Parties arrested on suspicion seem to have no trouble in proving their innocence." In June a young man named Delare was arrested at the Polk City depot and, "under threat of lynching", confessed to a gang plot that named a Missourian, Wickes, as the killer. In December John Weir was arrested and said he had driven William Kline and a man named Wilcox to Polk City to rob Stubbs, and that Kline admitted the killing.

The episode reached readers mainly through brief telegraphic items printed from Illinois and Dakota to Maine and Wyoming on April 18 and 19. The first wires reported "Contradictory reports" of a lynching and denied it, and the Wheeling Intelligencer headlined the item "Lynching Probable" on the ground that one was likely if the murderer could be identified. The fuller dispatches called the men "murderers" before any trial and the crowd "vigilantes", described the train's seizure without criticism, and closed on the citizens' pleas for law; the Dakotaian reprinted the Associated Press version a day later.

The short wire said the mob "attempted to take them from the officers, but failed", while the two fuller accounts said one prisoner was actually taken off the cars, without saying how he was recovered. The prisoners' names also varied by wire, from Weise, Swin and Errikson to "John Owl, Jobe Wese and Charley Derickson."

bases: Vigilantes stopped a train and took one of the murder suspects off it in an attempt to lynch them, but no one was reported killed, so this is an attempted lynching (A3, A5, A2).

Two separately worded Des Moines dispatches, one from the National Associated Press (A3) and one carried in Portland (A5), agree that vigilantes boarded the train and took one prisoner off before being persuaded to let it go, and a third wire says the mob failed to take the prisoners (A2, A7).
